Lascaux. A cave in southwestern France containing some of the world's finest Paleolithic wall paintings, created roughly seventeen thousand years ago during the Upper Paleolithic period. Its vivid polychrome murals of horses, bison, deer, and abstract symbols represent the artistic pinnacle of Ice Age hunter-gatherers and provide unparalleled evidence of aesthetic sophistication, symbolic thinking, and perhaps spiritual or shamanic beliefs in prehistoric humans.

Located in the Dordogne region of southwestern France, Lascaux was discovered accidentally in 1940 by teenagers and a dog. The narrow entrance had been sealed by rockfall for millennia, preserving the paintings in remarkable condition. The cave contains approximately six hundred paintings and fifteen hundred engravings covering roughly seventeen thousand square meters of wall space, the vast majority of which remain where they were first painted.

The paintings use natural earth pigments—charcoal, iron oxide, manganese dioxide—applied with fingers, brushes made from plant material, and possibly blown through tubes to create spray patterns. The images depict predominantly large herbivores, with horses being the most common, followed by bison, deer, and ibex, occasionally with predators and very few human figures, contrary to common misconception.

The famous Hall of the Bulls features four enormous aurochs, or wild cattle, some reaching up to seventeen feet long—the largest known Paleolithic paintings ever discovered. Certain panels appear to be astronomically aligned to celestial events, suggesting seasonal gatherings or ritual calendars encoded in the paintings themselves. Due to irreversible algae and fungal damage caused by visitor breath and body heat, the cave was closed to the general public in 1963. A full-scale replica, Lascaux IV, opened in 2016, allowing continued study and allowing modern visitors to appreciate these Ice Age masterworks that testify to the early emergence of human creativity and symbolic thinking.
